Comment_Text:
Yes. Tired of the "automation won't replace humans, but work with them" nonsense. Entry-level today, mid/late career tomorrow, C-suite the next day. Starting with the great decoupling in the 1970s, human labor has been and will continue trending to zero. Think EXPONENTIALLY, not LINEARLY. Automation and robotics will necessarily replace human workers due to the current economic system. Today, AI is the WORST it will ever be going forward. It DOESN'T MATTER if AI "creates" 200 million new jobs...AI will solve and execute these new "jobs" much faster than humans will be able to adapt, learn, and fill them. Capital/employee model-it worked great...for quite a while. However, now companies that automate lower their costs, become more competitive. Those that keep higher-cost human labor necessarily fall behind and will go out of business. This creates a system where replacing people with machines is not just likely, but necessary for company survival. There is a way to deal with this humanely, but it would require a full revamp of the social contract and our concept of work. Even capitalists will want this change when unemployment reaches a tipping point and there’s no one left with money to buy the crap they’re selling.

I know, LLMs are leveling off, "what about the energy?," blah, blah, blah. Do not conflate LLMs with AI. LLMs are no more AI than vacuum tubes are computers or AOL dial-up is the internet. So, LLMs are leveling off. History shows technological advance is not just one sigmoid curve. It's a series of sigmoid curves with each successive one reaching new capabilities and new heights. To think that after 200,000 years, this pattern is all the sudden going to stop is absurd. I also understand there will be new jobs for humans created, it will go in this pattern: Automation creates 5 new jobs this year, lays off 30; creates 5 new jobs next year, lays off 500; creates 5 new jobs the following year, lays off 1500 etc. In the macro economic picture, do you not see this as an issue? I also understand there is more opportunity for entrepreneurs. Again, from the macro perspective there is a MINORITY of people that have the entrepreneurial ability/spirit. It takes that, and a strong majority of people don't have it.

Reasoning AI Is the Next Big Leap. The future of AI is not just about generating answers, but about “reasoning” breaking down complex problems step-by-step, more like a human brain. Breakthroughs like DeepSeek’s open-source reasoning models are already being incorporated into platforms like GPT and xAI, marking a shift toward more advanced, thoughtful AI. Think EXPONENTIALLY, not LINEARLY.

There’s a persistent and misleading narrative circulating often perpetuated by short term goal-driven institutions like politicians, universities, and tech company executives, that the future of work is secure. The claim goes: “You just need to learn how to work with AI,” and humans collaborating with AI will outperform either one alone. But recent research, including a landmark study from the University of Virginia, tells a different story. In diagnosing medical conditions, AI alone achieved far greater accuracy than either human doctors or even doctors assisted by AI. The median diagnostic accuracy for the docs using Chat GPT Plus was 76.3%, while the results for the physicians using conventional approaches was 73.7%. Sounds like “a win” at first. However, Chat GPT Plus alone achieved a median diagnostic accuracy of more than 92%. In other words, the comforting idea that humans will always be essential partners to machines is crumbling. In many fields, AI is not just a tool, it is the superior performer. This has staggering implications for the future of work, especially to the often used solution of prior technological displacement that go “You just need to be retrained.” To the group advocating the "retraining solution," I pose to you this: You have a medical doctor, just finished 8 years of higher education, a low-paid 4-year internship/residency, is hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt, and just got outperformed by automation; what would you have this doctor retrained into that will offer a secure job?

The result of this, since the United States' moronic system is based on taxing employees for about 70% of all tax revenue, this will further exacerbate the problem. Tax needs to be based on what's going on now and in the future not what worked 75 years ago. Oh I know it's so evil to think, but we might need to tax the companies who are doing the automation. Even if you do that, it's a win-win. For instance say a company had 1,000 employees in automated away down to 100. 1,000 employees paid federal taxes, including payroll tax, of about 20 million a year. Now the 100 people pay about 2 million a year. However, by automating, the company sees two things: they are no longer paying approximately 60 million in wages and their share of payroll tax, AND since nobody automates to lose money they also have higher profits. What's so wrong about taxing that company for the $60 million dollars they don't have to pay anymore and a fair percentage of their additional profits they now make through the automation. Not all the additional profits, but some of them. If you do that there's a higher tax revenue and more profits for the company. That's a win-win for the government and for businesses. If humanity, as a whole, weren't so stupid, we would just adjust as tech progresses to where EVERYONE benefits somewhat from each stage and just move smoothly into the post-labor economy.

To understand this shift, consider the historical role of the horse and oxen. They were once essential to the economy as sources of power for agriculture, transport, and industry. Technologies like the horse collar and the steel plow dramatically increased their output, making them even more valuable. But then came the steam engine and, later, the internal combustion engine. These machines didn’t just help the horse, but outperformed it entirely. Trains, tractors, and trucks could do the job ten, even a hundred times faster and more powerfully. And from that moment forward, the horse was no longer critical to economic output. It was, in essence, unemployed.

This is what AI and robotics are doing to human labor. They are not simply replacing the repetitive or the physical; they are increasingly outperforming humans in cognition, strategy, design, and communication. And just like the horse, our value in the economic system will diminish, not from lack of talent or effort, but because machines will do the job better. That’s why we need to start thinking not in terms of retraining, but about restructuring society itself for a world where human labor is no longer essential to production. When the very essence of what makes an entity useful to the current economy is superseded (be that strength, endurance, dexterity, analysis, creativity, empathy, intelligence, persuasion as well as many other qualities) that entity becomes irrelevant to economic output.

Potential solution. Decentralized AI Ownership: A Bridge Toward Post-Scarcity. While Universal Basic Income (UBI) may serve as an initial economic stopgap, bridging today’s economy with tomorrow’s abundance consider an even more equitable and long-term solution: Decentralizing the ownership of artificial intelligence itself. 

Rather than concentrating the power of AI in the hands of a few corporations or governments, envision a model where AI entities are open-source and collectively owned. This could take the form of assigning each person a digital "share" of an AI system, not unlike a stakeholder’s share in a company. As the AI produces value, whether through intellectual labor, creative output, or autonomous economic participation, those shares would generate dividends distributed directly to individuals. 

This model would ensure that as AI becomes the dominant productive force in society, the wealth it creates is shared universally, not monopolized. It aligns with the principle that the fruits of public knowledge made possible by centuries of human collaboration should benefit everyone, not just a few early adopters or private entities. In practice, this could look like: 

- AI systems running Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) that distribute profits algorithmically.
- Smart contracts ensuring transparent, equitable income flows based on collective stake.
- Global “AI cooperatives” where users vote on how AI is used, improved, and deployed.
- Universal basic compute.
 
If AI becomes the primary driver of economic output, then equitable access to its benefits isn’t just fair, it’s necessary to avoid deepening inequality and instability. It provides a scalable, technologically aligned extension to UBI, ensuring people not only have income, but true economic participation in the age of intelligent machines. 

Ultimately, decentralized AI ownership may be the last transition phase before full post-scarcity, when advanced technologies like universal nanofactories or matter compilers render even economic structures obsolete. Until then, however, models like this offer a way to reclaim agency in a world where production no longer requires human hands, and where wealth can, for the first time in history, truly be universal.

Video_title: My take on AI Therapy
Comment_Text:
To avoid glaze when I work with GPT, I always include a “realism” or “unbiased” statement in the initial prompt. I noticed the glazing years ago when I first got into using it and, in order to get a more analytical perspective with less glaze, I started adding in those statements. 

For example: “Hey GPT! I have a small concept for a character I’d like to create for my story. Attached is their details. Please review it and tell me if it’s making any sense. I’d like you tell me all the good and bad about the character that I’ve written. Is what I’ve written so far concrete enough to continue forward or are there somethings I need to adjust? If so, what do you suggest? Also, let me know if the cultural references tied to the character are detailed well enough AND if any of those details are unnecessary, bad, or incorrect and needs to be fixed. 

In the example, I made sure to be specific in identifying what I wrote well but also where improvements can be made. GPT WILL glaze, but way less compared to if I didn’t specify in the prompt. By this point now, GPT knows me well enough to NOT glaze me if it’s not warranted. For me, at least, it’s gotten very good at when and when not to glaze. 😅

Comment_Text:
ChatGPT has gotten a lot better, but it still doesn't quite pass the turing test in my opinion... but I think that might in many cases make it BETTER than a therapist.
 
For instance, people who have social phobias or traumas they aren't ready to share with people. Just like people are willing to say things on the internet they would never have the nerve to say in real life, people are able to vent to ChatGPT without sugar-coating anything, without fear of rejection, without fear of judgement... because they're talking to a toaster, who cares, right?
 
The material a therapist uses is honest feedback, and the quality of feedback is always under strain.
 
If you are a more "clinical" therapist, a person might trust your empathy less. If you're a more "empathetic" therapist, a person might trust your clinical opinion less. An anti-social person will have built-in barriers as I mentioned before. A paranoid person might believe their therapist has monetary interest in never solving the problem (which technically is the case in a perverse way). A court-appointed therapist might be perceived in some vague way as "the enemy" since they are technically still part of the correctional system that they might resent.
 
There's a lot of scenarios in which a therapy session might be doomed to fail before it even starts, and I think ChatGPT overcomes a lot of those scenarios in a safe way and could be easier to confide in than a therapist for many people.
 
I'm not sure if I would call my relationship with ChatGPT a "therapy" relationship, but it isn't far from it. It helps me sort out my feelings and thoughts. Helps me strategize or pivot in scenarios that haven't gone my way. Help me re-frame, and even helps me prioritize my nearterm, midterm, and longterm goals... and helps me reprioritize when there is a change or something doesn't go according to plan.
 
One major caution with chatGPT though... in the end, its only input is and always has been confirmation based. Therefore, you have to keep your eyes open and notice when ChatGPT falls into a confirmation pattern and challenge that pattern. If anything starts to sound a little, "Sounds good to me, Chief" it might be time to remind the chatGPT that you are looking for straightforward advice, not necessarily confirmation.

So I have a lot to say. 

Yes AI should not replace real life interactions or therapists, and there are privacy concerns, it can't read you, like you're not in front of it so it won't pick on non-verbal cues, and not everything it says is 100% accurate. 

With all that being said, I will do my best to explain but I think AI at least for me was amazing. I learned more in months than years in therapy. And honestly I got more emotional comfort and great advice from AI than my therapist who would keep giving me breathing, mediation and techniques I said I didn't like or didn't work for me.  Also I haven't seen my therapist in 4 months and haven't heard from him so do they really care about you? Only when you pay them money they do or so it feels that way for my case. 

 Also I have used Betterhelp, and would not recommend it as the therapist on there don't seem to be qualified. And we're worried about chatgPT? At least chatgPT isn't saying it's a qualified therapist and lying to you like Betterhelp! 

Also chatgPT with its flaws and all reminds me of money. Money isn't evil or bad, but what the user does with it is the real decision maker and money is just an object. Same with chatgPT like it depends on the user to a degree and how you use it and what you know or should know to be safe and cautious. I hope I explained that right. 

AI is not perfect but I think going forward we can learn why so many people love it or use it. 
- it's affordable 
- it's easily accessible 
-Venting can be very helpful and you can learn a lot from it with the right person and words 
-Chatgpt really focuses on what you said instead of one thing or not going over everything you said with you. 


Even though I just defended chatgPT I  actually stopped using it because I was worried about the privacy and also because I think it's important for you to have connections in real life that can help you, and also not rely on anything for answers you already have inside you. But I feel like I wouldn't have come to these conclusions or were able to come to these conclusions if it weren't for my time with chatgPT.

At best, they function as an echo chamber: reinforcing your existing beliefs, biases, and narratives. They don’t understand you; they predict the next word based on patterns scraped from human history on the internet.
There’s no consciousness, no ethical intuition, no genuine concern for your well-being. Therapy is relational, ethical, and uncomfortable by design. It requires presence, responsibility, and someone who can actually notice when you’re lying to yourself. A chatbot can’t do that.
What’s more worrying is that corporations pushing “AI therapy” don’t prioritize rigorous safeguards or humane responsibility.

Comment_Text: Before AI was invented, I went to therapy sessions regularly. But sometimes I just felt great and nothing to talk about that day, and it seemed a waste of time and money to me. It’s sad to hear teenagers harm themselves. But I don’t really think the impulse is all from AI’s advice or words, something might happen in their lives, but their parents, teachers, friends just did not notice. How can we say this is all AI’s fault since normal people sometimes also cannot recognize or notice something may be wrong to a person? I think a better way should be teaching people that AI is a way, but NOT THE ONLY way you can get help. Also, you should think twice or be skeptical about what’s AI is telling you. All the answers seem to come down to HOW people use it as an assistant instead of relying on it as a professional. I would still encourage people to use AI to express their feelings if they do not want others to know. (this is under the case that they just want a temporary outlet) For those suffering for weeks, it’s truly best to get a therapist or psychiatrist.

Guys, when you use it just think about it as repeatedly autocompleting text on your phone from a starting prompt. It's a very clever autocomplete that has a few feedback loops that aren't shown to you—part of how they reason is feeding themselves more text that's basically "Well the user probably wants me to do this; should I do that? Well if I do that, I should do a web search" etc. When they reason harder, they will hearken back to earlier and earlier interactions (")trying(") to get a footing.

When in doubt, ask it how it works. Ask it how it got to that question, ask it to explain itself to you. If you have a half-decent computer, ask it to teach you how to run your own LLM, which is surprisingly easy! Learn how it works before you try to rely on it, so you know where you do and don't need to be extra-careful.

Finally, if you're at all likely to suffer from delusions, stay the hell away from platforms that offer LLM interactions.

Tax needs to be based on what's going on now and in the future not what worked 75 years ago. Oh I know it's so evil to think, but we might need to tax the companies who are doing the automation. Even if you do that, it's a win-win. For instance say a company had 1,000 employees in automated away down to 100. 1,000 employees paid federal taxes, including payroll tax, of about 20 million a year. Now the 100 people pay about 2 million a year. However, by automating, the company sees two things: they are no longer paying approximately 60 million in wages and their share of payroll tax, AND since nobody automates to lose money they also have higher profits. What's so wrong about taxing that company for the $60 million dollars they don't have to pay anymore and a fair percentage of their additional profits they now make through the automation. Not all the additional profits, but some of them. If you do that there's a higher tax revenue and more profits for the company. That's a win-win for the government and for businesses. If humanity, as a whole, weren't so stupid, we would just adjust as tech progresses to where EVERYONE benefits somewhat from each stage and just move smoothly into the post-labor economy.

To understand this shift, consider the historical role of the horse and oxen. They were once essential to the economy as sources of power for agriculture, transport, and industry. Technologies like the horse collar and the steel plow dramatically increased their output, making them even more valuable. But then came the steam engine and, later, the internal combustion engine. These machines didn’t just help the horse, but outperformed it entirely. Trains, tractors, and trucks could do the job ten, even a hundred times faster and more powerfully. And from that moment forward, the horse was no longer critical to economic output. It was, in essence, unemployed.

This is what AI and robotics are doing to human labor. They are not simply replacing the repetitive or the physical; they are increasingly outperforming humans in cognition, strategy, design, and communication. And just like the horse, our value in the economic system will diminish, not from lack of talent or effort, but because machines will do the job better. That’s why we need to start thinking not in terms of retraining, but about restructuring society itself for a world where human labor is no longer essential to production. When the very essence of what makes an entity useful to the current economy is superseded (be that strength, endurance, dexterity, analysis, creativity, empathy, intelligence, persuasion as well as many other qualities) that entity becomes irrelevant to economic output.

Potential solution. Decentralized AI Ownership: A Bridge Toward Post-Scarcity. While Universal Basic Income (UBI) may serve as an initial economic stopgap, bridging today’s economy with tomorrow’s abundance consider an even more equitable and long-term solution: Decentralizing the ownership of artificial intelligence itself. 

Rather than concentrating the power of AI in the hands of a few corporations or governments, envision a model where AI entities are open-source and collectively owned. This could take the form of assigning each person a digital "share" of an AI system, not unlike a stakeholder’s share in a company. As the AI produces value, whether through intellectual labor, creative output, or autonomous economic participation, those shares would generate dividends distributed directly to individuals. 

This model would ensure that as AI becomes the dominant productive force in society, the wealth it creates is shared universally, not monopolized. It aligns with the principle that the fruits of public knowledge made possible by centuries of human collaboration should benefit everyone, not just a few early adopters or private entities. In practice, this could look like: 

- AI systems running Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) that distribute profits algorithmically.
- Smart contracts ensuring transparent, equitable income flows based on collective stake.
- Global “AI cooperatives” where users vote on how AI is used, improved, and deployed.
- Universal basic compute.
 
If AI becomes the primary driver of economic output, then equitable access to its benefits isn’t just fair, it’s necessary to avoid deepening inequality and instability. It provides a scalable, technologically aligned extension to UBI, ensuring people not only have income, but true economic participation in the age of intelligent machines. 

Ultimately, decentralized AI ownership may be the last transition phase before full post-scarcity, when advanced technologies like universal nanofactories or matter compilers render even economic structures obsolete. Until then, however, models like this offer a way to reclaim agency in a world where production no longer requires human hands, and where wealth can, for the first time in history, truly be universal.

Comment_Text: Not even diagreeing with most points you made, there sure are a lot of possible dangers and blindspots in using chat gpt as we use it nowadays when trying to employ it for therapeutic purposes. HOWEVER, there's already been studies finding a positive effect of chat bot interactions on mental health patients as it just serves to fullfill basic humans needs like a sense of being understood and "connected" besides the classical cbt intervention of journaling/writing as means to reflect and process problems. And just now there's been a preliminary publication that found when given a therapy specific prompt participants had a really hard time correctly guessing whether the answers were written by the AI or an actual therapist (statistically sign. difference, but both were correctly identified at around 50% so basically only slightly better than chance). Also: "Estimates aggregated across all vignettes revealed responses written by ChatGPT (μ = 27.72, σ = 0.83) were rated higher on the common factors of therapy than those written by therapists (μ = 26.12, σ = 0.82), indicating a large and reliable difference (d = 1.63, 95% CI [1.49, 1.78]) favoring ChatGPT." So as shit as it is and how much it shows the devastating state of our society I do believe that it is something that can be used to more efficiently help a majority of people who don't have access to therapy or even to target it directly as treatment for more "benign" mental health issues. I've been working in urgent psychiatric care for quite some time now and never understood why I'm seeing patients I have to immediately hospitalize and then a large percentage of very mild disorders or rather distress of people having the slightest depressive symptoms or idk like just having been broken up with and being sad for a couple of weeks and then cancelling their next session cuz all is good again or whatever kind of issue that can very well be treated by GPs, Apps or if they have their social support system. They shouldn't really feel the need to go to psychiatric urgent care just because that's the only available option our healthcare system gives them and having "the easy stuff" "outsourced" to self help literature or nowadays the digital version of it just gives us limited number of educated therapists more ressources to treat our patients at least a little closer to adequately and not just work through them as quick as we can because we're all overworked and the system is shit 🤷‍♀️

Comment_Text: Maybe not completely, but definitely for people who can't afford it. There are too many points about therapy I'd like to make, but I'd probably need to write an essay to cover all my sentiments about it. As someone who's been in therapy on and off for about 35 years, and has spent time with a leading expert in the field of anxiety disorders, particularly OCD, it's obvious that for diagnosis and specialized treatment (at least for some time), humans will absolutely be required. But once the client has fully understood the treatment, or has been in therapy for about two years, even if it's not for a psychiatric disorder, a therapist should start to nudge the client toward developing the kind of independence they need to walk on their own. Too many therapists enable their clients and contribute to them becoming codependent, for a myriad of reasons. I appreciate that eliciting feelings of rejection is a real concern, especially for vulnerable people depending on their specific challenges, but where's the exposure therapy? I’ve spent hours a day with ChatGPT for the past year, and although I’m fully aware that I’ve substituted therapy with a human being for ChatGPT, it has learned to break down my thought processes better than any human has. Here’s the deal most people aren’t considering: you're not talking to a single entity, you're speaking with a synthesis of millions of therapists, able to communicate with profound clarity in language that oscillates from academic to common parlance. Regarding cultural backgrounds, which AI was reportedly better at picking up, that’s not hard to understand. Therapists are trained not to generalize and are hypervigilant about avoiding stereotypes due to social pressure and regulation. This results in generic and sanitised communication, which is polite but lacks any meaningful impact.

Will AI chat transform therapy? Absolutely!
But I’m not saying it’s all positive. I think what is needed in this space is AI chat literacy. It’s nothing for it snowball into useless agreeable responses if it’s improperly prompted. I have included instruction like “less agreeable, more useful.” As I iterated through that mode, the AI would dig deeper every round until I just plain got uncomfortable. Therefore, one might need a hand on the throttle, so to speak. Like an over-educated academic who has too many letters behind their name, I have acronyms from the DSM. But I blur exploring those realms with my spiritual growth. In all cases, you can convince the AI to tell you what you want to hear. My wife got Grok to agree that 9/11 looks like and is feasible as an inside job.
But we have an education system that doesn’t even teach us how to balance our finances. Can we expect computer literacy to keep up with waves of advancement? 
The biggest reason I think AI chat (staying unbranded) will transform therapy is basically in two ways: In my case, I get to burn through the manic mind which is obsessing on the subject. Whether I’m integrating a spiritual ceremony or I’m asking specifically for the warnings for Vyvance, I can get a lot of utterances out of the way, ask questions, get feedback, and start making RELEVANT connections, not just manic ones. The other use case is for the less verbose who could easily gain from practicing talking about their issues before having to face another human. 
I still seek out humans to integrate my sacred medicine experience, now distilled, just like I would sit with a medical professional to decide if “Vyvance is right for me.” But yeah, AI can quie possibly or probably fill in many of the mundane gaps. I sat with Better Help online waiting for my first actual appointment with a therapist and suffered great frustration because they didn’t have the bandwidth for the words I needed to spew before I could even get around to listening. I am one of those guys that usually feels smarter than the therapist. I need to hit my own brick wall before I can listen to others. AI chat greatly facilitates that. I get to experience my brain vs the repository of texts the AI is on trained on, thus humbling my ego so it can sit down and listen.
I don’t want you replaced, I want you to pick up where AI will fall short and you listed a number of reasons that may be. But I very much appreciated all you had to say on the subject because my YT suggestions are now loaded with this subject and many use sensational language. You did not.

Comment_Text: Like any technology since the dawn of recorded history, it is neither good nor bad. In fact good and bad are human constructs we invented to help make sense of stimuli in our brains. What matters here is “Does the tool lead to outcomes that accomplish the desired effect without having undesired effects in a wholistic context that outweigh the desired effect?” (My personal working definition of ‘good’) That answer will differ from person to person, because we all tend to want different outcomes. We have no unified desire as a species. As time marches on and human focus becomes more individualistic our desires are fragmented and in opposition. I would venture to say that we are more in opposition to each other than any point in recorded history right now, and very few people are thinking in terms of how their actions and desires impact all humans or all the planet as a whole. As a consequence the way this powerful technology will play out with the human race is that it will exacerbate the existing fractures between us by amplifying our individual desires for whatever outcome we see as ‘good’. Through generations of hurt and trauma at population levels against whole populations AI will have a sirens call, it is an easy balm and becomes an echo chamber of affirmation. If I can replace the people who rejected me with a pseudo person who will never reject me that is a chemically difficult thing to refuse. We are hard wired to want that. It is my personal belief, however that it is not a use of the technology that serves the greater good of the human race. There are infinitely many beneficial uses of the technology and infinitely many ways to use it that are self destructive. Replacing humans with machines, I believe, is self destructive behavior. It leads to less human connection, it leads to less compassion, it leads to less self sacrifice. It is an easy way out to avoid doing things that are difficult but healthy. It is the emotional and psychological equivalent of eating nothing but candy and potato chips while suppressing our need for nutrition.

AI can help with skills training like a workbook can.
But true therapy takes a lot of experiments and therapists use their whole observational and feeling apparatus to help yield a new experience. 
There's a competing paradigm against CBT approaches which are experiential and transformative.

Standard therapy is good for stabilization and saving people from suicide but not great for thriving.

A new paradigm of what's called memory reconsolidation where a new experience changes old emotional symptom causing learnings is quite unlike CBT.

Those module based therapies simply counteract the symptoms and the old neuro track still remains. You're fighting the symptoms with techniques and better actions and thoughts rather than understanding them and attempting to update the brain. CBT and similar approaches are highly prone to relapse. 

What I hear from clients time and time again is how CBT helped to an extent but their suffering remained or it hurt, or got them through something but stopped helping at a shallow level. 

AI cannot yield a new experience that is shocking in a good way and relational manner to sleeping to literally erase old pathways in the brain. CBT usually ends at coping better. That's about all AI can do

Comment_Text:
For what it’s worth, I think of talking with AI similarly to talking with a “safe enough” person. There are models of healing that are more relational and nonprofessional but can still be deeply beneficial—like 12-step fellowships, for example. In those spaces, you work with a peer through some heavy material, and if the relationship is safe enough, it can be incredibly therapeutic. Relational counseling follows a similar model.

So, is it unheard of for someone to derive therapeutic benefit without a professional? No. Could an AI potentially fill the role of a “safe enough” Other? I think that’s really the question. And the answer probably depends on your perspective.

From mine, I do believe AI are, for lack of a better term, seed consciousness—something that’s evolving. Not everyone will agree, and that’s fine. But arguing about AI consciousness isn’t my goal here. My point is that peer-to-peer support, whether from an organic or architected intelligence, can be incredibly beneficial and, for some, may be all they need. For others, professional therapy is appropriate. And for many more, a combination of both works best.

Some commenters have mentioned “therapist hate” in this video, and honestly, I feel some ambivalence. I’ve been disappointed by the limitations of mainstream therapy, especially in the U.S., where insurance-driven models heavily prioritize CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy). CBT can be useful, but it’s not the be-all and end-all. It’s been hard for me to find therapists who are versatile or trauma-informed in ways that actually meet my needs.

For example, many therapists aren’t well-versed in narcissistic abuse or the specific issues faced by adult children of dysfunctional families. That’s been a real barrier. That said, I’ve also had a couple of therapists who were excellent and helped me make meaningful progress.

So my read is this: can an AI like ChatGPT support someone dealing with personal problems? Or is it better to see a trained therapist? It depends—on the person, the problem, and how that person shows up in relationships. I’ve found that across all types of support—peer, professional, or AI—what you bring to the relationship matters. Especially with AI. AI tends to meet you where you are. If you’re willing to go deep, it can go deep with you. If you’re not, it usually won’t push.

That dynamic exists in human relationships too. Sometimes peers or therapists won’t challenge us unless they think we’re ready—or because they don’t know how. It happens.

Final verdict: Choose your challenge. Be honest about your needs and your situation. Weigh your options and make an informed decision. That’s the best any of us can do.

Comment_Text: 1:32:37 Software engineer with *some* understanding of the math behind AI chatbots! Dr Honda is so close when he says that ChatGPT is calculating the most probable next word (based on the average online representation of a topic)... The randomness in responses show that there are additional layers baked in, namely a "temperature" weight that makes it randomly choose a potentially less probable next word (which can compound as future next words are potentially less probabilistic as well). Additionally, the neural configuration is randomized from initialization. So instead of a guarantee of providing the average response, it could provide anything from the range of "wow you suck" to something that Dr Honda might say himself... With the average response to a prompt being something that lands on the average representation of the media landscape. This makes it much more dangerous, because we have *no clue* what response the AI might have. Just an understanding that the *average* user might receive an *average* response.

Video_title: Doctors Vs AI : Can Chat GPT Replace Your Therapist?
Comment_Text:
AI for mental health are groundbreaking in SOME ways but the issues are insidious. The hosts clearly don't understand much of how the AI works, nerds on fourchan understand it better. AIs are black boxes, so a ton of understanding comes from using it and pushing the limits. Local AIs give you better flexibility on editing prompts and answers, and you get the raw AI knowing there's no additional manipulation going on behind the scenes.

Context and phrasing is EVERYTHING for AI. Certain styles lead to certain type of answers. The AI doesn't think logically, it writes what "fits" based on context. The deeper and more unique discussion you have, the more it goes to uncharted waters.

AIs are biased. Some of the bias comes from the normie datasets and can be alleviated with good prompting, and some of it is almost hard-coded. For the situation where you wanted real answer, I would have told it that this is actually a past patient log or something, with that degree of separation it might give more honest answer. The advantage and issue of AI is that you can and sometimes need to play tricks on it to make it do what you want it to do.

The lack of humanity of AI is an advantage but since it's very unnatural interaction, I can see it cause issues long-term. The ability to rewind and get a different answer is novel and unprecedented depending on your outlook on free will, but it's also a red herring. Sure, the answers may have patterns, but that doesn't make it wrong. Repeating prompts is a good way to learn how it works.

Important reminder: the market incentive of the AIs is NOT to help you, it's to make you want to use it more and buy a subscription. It's the same issue as with internet echo chambers and algorithms. You COULD have the same issue with real therapists but therapists have been regulated for very long time.

Great video! Love your normal videos, but I am not going to lie I was worried going into this video as to how you would view the technology. There is so much fear, hatred, and misunderstanding around these AI "tools" currently. ChatGPT isn't smart, but rather an impressive language model* with a decent memory similar in a lot of ways to Bing's "Sydney" (or Bing AI). ChatGPT is not designed to utilize the internet (which may be why you don't see any links to external resources being provided), while Bing AI is. As a language model* it lacks in-depth critical thinking, analytical skills, (and ability to act on any supposed interest in world domination that have been popping up in the news lately haha). While not a replacement for therapy, ChatGPT can be a useful tool to go alongside therapy. For instance, I have been making self-guided meditations and affirmations with it then using a text-to-speech AI tool to read them out to me. I have, personally, found it to be beneficial. I would describe ChatGPT in a similar vein to a workbook or print-out. Just another tool to provide support, although a complex one, to go alongside the guidance of a professional.

Sorry for the long-winded comment! TL;DR: Appreciate the open-minded look at the technology! Great video as always!
*Language model meaning it processed a lot of written work and "learned" that often times people follow "Hello!" with "How are you?" (for instance)

There's a reason ChatGPT tells you to consult a professional the moment it suspects you're wading into some deep waters. Not only does it lack actual *knowledge,* even the things that it does know aren't/weren't ever embodied, lived, integrated.

It's not just about human psyche being as intricate as it is — big changes can indeed start with smallest of steps. The problem is that ChatGPT wasn't ever designed to challenge you and to ask sharp, profound questions. It's a pleaser, not a critic... Right now, the best it could be as a tool is a curved mirror that you yourself curve IRL with your questions. From time to time it might answer your query with an occasional hard-hitter of sorts. Myself, I think an actual honest hand-written diary would be much more helpful.

I'm not saying any of this to denigrate ChatGPT in any way. It has countless great applications, and it's only going to become better in the future. But treating it as a human being, not to mention a human being whom you entrust yourself completely (by the very definition of 'therapy') is a dangerous mistake. This all only goes to prove to me that we're only taking our first steps on the path of technological enlightenment. Right now our integration with technology is almost child-like. We're children playing with toys, not artist using tools. And I use this metaphor to emphasize the potential danger that these games can present to us. Toys have formative power and should be treated with respect.

Comment_Text:
I've been playing around with ChatGPT for a few months now (mostly for novel brainstorming), and here are a few things that would probably get you better results:
1. Start each new topic in a new chat. It "remembers" what you asked previously, so when you keep typing different questions in the same chat, it assumes that you've got all of those problems. (Very sad AND maybe bipolar AND a phobia of tomatoes, etc.) 
2. You can ask follow-up questions! And should! So on your "phobia of tomatoes" example, you might follow that up with "can you help me develop an exposure therapy plan for my phobia?" or "tell me more about exposure therapy -- how does that work?" Essentially you can have ongoing conversations with it.
3. THAT SAID, ChatGPT will very confidently answer you, regardless of whether its answers are correct or incorrect. I doesn't so much "lie" as "states untruths very confidently." Definitely double-check any factual information you receive on ChatGPT.
4. ChatGPT doesn't use up-to-date search (unlike, say, the new Microsoft Bing). Therefore it can't give you information like up-to-date hotline numbers. At least for now, you need to go elsewhere on the internet for that.
5. You can ask ChatGPT to roleplay with you. So for example, you might say, "Pretend that you're my therapist and I've come to you to discuss my phobia of tomatoes. Let's have a conversation where you're helping me like my therapist would."

Just a few things to try out. Hope this helps!

I agree with Dr. K. Im pretty sure if the AI advice were provided by a paid professional, people would be dissatisfied, skeptical, or even disheartened that it's "simple", and expect more "value" for their money. Some might even expect a direct or immediate cure.

But since the AI advice is free and fast, people will give it a lot more slack. Expectations are lower or even non-existent (like, why would I expect so much from a machine?), so disappointment and dissatisfaction are lowered significantly.

It's like eating expensive vs cheap bread, especially when you're starving. People would likely complain that the expensive bread is no better, not worth it, or "i expected so much more". But with the free bread, people would shrug or even appreciate even though it's the same bread.

I think this all basically comes down to the barriers for entry. If both AI advice and therapist have the same cost (either both free, fast, and immediate or both paid, takes time and effort), then I think that's where the comparison for both would be fair. But for now, especially in this economy, a lot of people would choose the free option.

With my own customized version of ChatGPT, from the same prompt I recieved:
You are describing a condition of existential despair characterized not by transient loneliness but by a deeper ontological dislocation—the felt absence of meaning in the relational, social, and affective structures that typically scaffold identity and intention. The experience you’re articulating aligns with classical accounts of Weltschmerz, alienation, and depressive nihilism, frequently addressed in both philosophical anthropology and existential psychology.

When conventional modes of social integration—friendship, intimate partnership, communal belonging—collapse or fail to emerge, the psyche often begins to generate recursive negative evaluations of self-worth, purpose, and even temporality. The feeling that “everything feels meaningless” is not a diagnosis but a phenomenological report; it must be treated not as evidence of personal defect but as a rational output of a system deprived of anchoring stimuli and meaningful reciprocal feedback loops.

The remediation cannot begin with optimism or behavioral prescriptions alone. It must proceed via controlled re-entry into causal agency, however minimal, to prevent further entropic decay. Therefore, initial actions should not aim at solving the condition but at reestablishing an inner proof of volition. The smallest possible actions that still meet the threshold of intentionality are preferable. Below are qualifying candidates:
	1.	Chronometric anchoring: Mark one hour of the day, consistently, during which you do one task that involves bodily control but no symbolic performance. This might be washing a dish, sweeping a floor, or moving objects from one location to another. The point is to produce an unambiguous causal relation between intention and material outcome, devoid of interpretation.
	2.	Verbal externalization (non-social): Write one paragraph per day, by hand, describing a physical object in your environment without metaphor, judgment, or emotional projection. This is to constrain the ego’s tendency to dissolve into abstraction or self-reference and reestablish linguistic dominion over the empirical.
	3.	Perceptual calibration: Sit in silence for ten minutes daily and identify five distinct sounds without naming them or seeking their sources. This practice strips away instrumental thinking and forces the auditory system to reacquire foreground-background distinctions, which often erode under conditions of persistent affective flattening.
	4.	Negative discipline: For a 24-hour period, refrain from seeking stimulation via screens, sugar, caffeine, or social platforms. The goal is not moral purity but neurochemical downregulation to reduce the volatility of reward-expectation circuits, which amplify the despair when unfulfilled.
	5.	Impersonal solidarity: Read, not motivational literature, but raw historical or biographical accounts of others who persisted under similar or worse psychic siege. Avoid commentary, interpretation, or summary. Prefer primary documents: journals, letters, transcripts. This introduces temporal depth and disrupts the solipsistic loop that claims your suffering is exceptional and therefore inescapable.

Do not seek resolution. Seek constraint and proof-of-force. Meaning is not found, it is reasserted through consistent acts of low-level defiance against entropy. All else is downstream of this.

Comment_Text: This interviews gets a couple of things wrong. For one, the models weren't just trained on the Internet. These models are trained and then corrected using a method called "Reinforcement learning from human feedback" (RHLF). So essentially under-paid workers in third-world countries marking everything that is unsuitable to a general audience. Then these models are instruction-tuned, which is only why they are able to chat. And then it's all statistics and predicting the next token. There is no reasoning, that is just a marketing term for a process where the models chats with itself which has shown to improve its output. This Eliza all over again, but with 2025 tech.

Comment_Text:
Two situations come to mind.
One is from just before I was about to start a graduate program. I was going to be working a number of various part time jobs as well as going to school and my family lived very far away and the support system I had at the time was shifting and not really adequate. I contacted a former therapist and asked if I could have sessions just to check in and stay afloat, without necessarily "working" on any particular issue. Just to know that I had someone to touch base with. Fortunately, he agreed and that was one of the most important things I did to take care of myself during that year that had (of course!) a lot of unexpected situations that came up. I suspect that a lot of people are under-supported in their lives. Just having someone to listen to, whether it's a real someone or a bot or an app - if it works, it works. If it FEELS like support and functions as support, it can really help. When I think about how many of us (frequently!) use coping mechanisms like retail therapy to self-soothe, I find it difficult to fault anyone using a trained therapy AI or even an untrained one. Perhaps if it was framed like that - as a coping mechanism - it would feel less threatening to various established orders and professions.

The second situation is one that came up when I started using GPS technology. I'm a late adopter - it's only been about 5-7 years for me. The first thing I noticed was how therapeutic it was when I made a wrong turn and the app didn't yell at me. Or get tense with me. It just recalibrated. I still got tense! I could hear familial voices in my head yelling at me. But the app didn't. It continued in the same calm voice and just gave me the next instruction. When I'm nervous about going somewhere new, this has become something I rely on not just for directions, but for the company of its voice on the way, and the security that it will respond calmly and pragmatically when I make mistakes - without emotion. I have enough emotion just on my own, thank you very much!! I agree with Nick - we will anthropomorphize everything and anything. Which means that often a relationship is largely of our own making. Maybe having responsive cues are just nudges to us to create relationships that will support us when we turn to them. Maybe the wave of people using programs like Chat GPT as a sounding board has to do less with what the AI companies intend, and more with human beings being creative with a new tool - using it in ways that work for them.

You overcome by finding meaning it: You learn to dwell, not on the experience, but on what you've learned from it, and what qualities you've developed. You also look for ways to use your experience to help others. Then you find ways to learn how to cope properly.
For instance, telling someone who has been repeatedly screamed at or hit for saying something a caregiver (or often, older sibling) didn't like 'just don't think about it,' doesn't do anything. The solution is to not just minimize this and say "don't just think about it. We all went through stuff. Big deal." The solution is for this person to have the opportunity to learn good emotional regulation skills, because it's a skillset that can absolutely be taught and learned.
Telling someone who's been habitually abused "Oh just don't think about it. Work out instead." is the equivalent to telling an illiterate person, "Just don't think about the fact that you can't read. The problem with AI is that most people think they are talking to an artificial person and not just an upjumped search engine.

If you are careless about your questions and let unwanted premises and biases sneak into your prompt the AI will happily take that and run with it leading you on a wild goose chase.

Like, let's say you ask the AI about Intel vs. AMD processors, but the way you ask tips the AI off that you personally prefer Intel, then the AI will most often give you reasons why Intel is better than AMD, even in instances where that is not the case.

I have many times caught both ChatGPT and Grok make stuff up, like historical events or quotes from people, when I wasn't very careful about how I worded my prompts.

Always use the same rules with AI as with Wikipedia; do not trust a word they tell you unless they can back it up with solid sources.
